newsitem.title: TAIWAN: S.Africa envoy hopes Taiwan won't avenge China snub.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa envoy hopes Taiwan won't avenge China snub.

text.p: South Africa's envoy to Taiwan said on Wednesday he hoped Taipei would not take reprisals against Pretoria for its decision to sever diplomatic ties with the island in favour of mainland China.

"I sincerely hope not," Ambassador Johannes Viljoen told Reuters when asked if an offended Taiwan might reduce or halt its substantial economic cooperation with South Africa or inflict other reprisals.
"We would like to retain our economic relations with Taiwan," he said shortly after learning of President Nelson Mandela's decision.

"Of course they are a very important trading partner of South Africa, our sixth largest, and also an important source of assistance. We sincerely hope the projects they have going in South Africa would continue."
Mandela told a news conference at his Johannesburg home that the process of recognising Beijing would be a gradual one that he hoped could be completed within a year.
"A permanent continuation of diplomatic recognition of the Republic of China on (the island of) Taiwan is inconsistent with South Africa's role in international affairs," Mandela said.
Taiwan government officials, apparently taken by surprise by the announcement, rushed past reporters at the Foreign Ministry late on Wednesday, refusing to comment.

Taiwan, seen by Beijing as a renegade province not entitled to sovereign foreign ties since a civil war split them in 1949, has tried to use its economic muscle to keep ties with the 30 states that still recognise it instead of Beijing.
South Africa was Taiwan's biggest diplomatic ally.
Viljoen said the diplomatic blow was unlikely to hurt Taiwan's economy, which has lost some of its "Asian dragon" fire in recent years and only lately begun mounting a comeback.
"Taiwan's economy is so strong and so resilient," he said.

"It was able to come out of a bigger crisis than this when the Americans broke off relations in the 1970s. That was a big thing and look how they progressed economically. I don't think this will have any effect on the Taiwanese economy," he said.

The United States recognised Beijing in 1979 but maintains extensive unofficial relations with Taiwan and reserves a right to arm and even defend the island in the interest of peaceful resolution of the half-century old Taiwan-China stalemate.

Viljoen said South Africa's shift toward recognising Beijing appeared to have begun in December 1995, when Mandela's African National Council leadership decided to send Foreign Minister Alfred Nzo to Beijing and Taipei to assess ties with both.
"From our side we would like to maintain good relations with both the People's Republic of China and the Republic of China and have always stated that," he said.
"How to achieve that has always been a problem. We just hope it will be possible to maintain substantial and friendly relations with Taiwan in the future."
